lessons.title: Hash Functions
intro: Searching a list means looking at every item. A hash table goes straight to the right place: a hash function turns the key, like a word, into a number, and that number is the index into an array.

A good hash function mixes all the letters, so similar words land in different places. A classic one: h = h * 31 + c for every character, then % SIZE to fit the table. Doing % SIZE at every step keeps the numbers small.
The same word always gives the same number. That's the whole trick: to find a word again, you calculate its hash and look in just that one place.

exercises.prompt: What does a hash function do?
options: Turns a key into an index in the table
exercises.explanation: Same key in, same index out, every time.

options: So the number fits into the table, from 0 to SIZE - 1
exercises.explanation: The remainder after dividing by SIZE is always smaller than SIZE.

exercises.prompt: Why is h = h + c (just adding the letters) a bad hash function?
options: "stop" and "pots" get the same number, because the order doesn't count
exercises.explanation: Multiplying by 31 makes the position of each letter count.

exercises.prompt: Two different words land on the same index. What is that called?
exercises.explanation: With more words than places, collisions can't be avoided. The next lesson handles them.

lessons.title: Buckets and Chains
intro: When two words land on the same index, they collide. The classic fix: every place in the table holds a linked list, called a chain or bucket. A word is added to the front of the list at its index.

To look a word up, calculate its hash, then walk only that one short list with strcmp. With a good hash function, the lists stay short, and a lookup takes about the same time for 10 words as for 10 million.
strdup(word) makes a copy of the word in fresh memory from malloc. The table needs its own copy, because the original buffer may be overwritten by the next word.

code: for (e = table[hash(word)]; e != NULL; e = e->next)
for (e = table[i]; e != NULL; e = e->next)

exercises.prompt: What's in each place of the table here?
options: A linked list of the entries with that hash
exercises.explanation: A list can hold any number of colliding words.

exercises.prompt: How does lookup find a word?
options: Calculate the hash, then walk only that one list with strcmp
exercises.explanation: That's why it's fast: most of the table is never touched.

exercises.prompt: Add the new entry to the front of its chain.
exercises.explanation: Point the new entry to the old first one, then make the new one first.

exercises.prompt: Why strdup(word) instead of e->word = word?
options: The table needs its own copy; the caller's buffer may change later
word can't be stored in a struct
exercises.explanation: Reading words into one buffer with scanf would otherwise make every entry point at the last word.

exercises.prompt: What does add("unix") return the second time it's called?
exercises.explanation: add first calls lookup, and only makes a new entry if the word is missing.

exercises.prompt: With a good hash function, how does a lookup's speed change from 1,000 to 1,000,000 words, if the table grows too?
exercises.explanation: The lists stay just as short: this is why hash tables are everywhere, from compilers to databases.

lessons.title: Counting Words
intro: Here's the hash table at work: read words with scanf("%s", buf), and count each one with add(buf)->count++.
This is the job a hash table was made for: compilers keep their variable names in one, spell checkers their words, and Unix's awk and Perl built their arrays on them.
To print the result, walk every place of the table and every entry in its chain.

code: for (e = table[hash(word)]; e != NULL; e = e->next)
for (e = table[i]; e != NULL; e = e->next)

exercises.prompt: Why does a new word have count 0 at first?
options: add sets count = 0, and the caller adds 1 after
exercises.explanation: That's how the example notices a word it hasn't seen before.

exercises.prompt: How many times does "the" appear in the example's input?
exercises.explanation: "the cat and the dog" has two, and "and the bird" one more.

exercises.prompt: Read one word at a time until the input ends.
exercises.explanation: scanf returns how many values it read: 1 while there are words left.

exercises.prompt: What would you need to print the words sorted by count?
options: Copy the entries into an array and qsort it
exercises.explanation: A hash table has no order. That's the chapter project.

options: Compilers' symbol tables, spell checkers, databases and dictionaries in Python
exercises.explanation: Python's dict and JavaScript's objects are hash tables underneath.

exercises.prompt: Why read each word into buf and not straight into the table?
options: You don't know yet if the word is new, so add() decides and makes a copy if needed
scanf can't write to a table
exercises.explanation: Only new words get their own memory.
